business: LavLav — a small nail & beauty studio (manicure, pedicure, brows/lamination, lashes, permanent makeup, laser) in the Master kvart building in Podgorica, whose booking already runs on DIKIDI; the page is an outreach concept whose only job is to introduce the studio and hand the visitor to that existing booking flow (src/app/(me)/demo/lavlav/data.ts header comment).
artDirection: A printed lookbook for a small studio, not a beauty-SaaS landing page: warm cream paper (#f2eee5) with a second, slightly deeper "shell" stock (#e8e2d6) for the gallery band, black ink, and exactly one lacquer red borrowed from the nails themselves. The whole page is flat — no rounded corners, no shadows, no cards; structure comes from full-width hairlines, band changes, and photography sitting directly on the paper. The tone is intimate and adult rather than cute or clinical: wide-tracked display type, captioned photographs, and an editorial restraint that assumes the reader recognises a good manicure without being sold one.
signatureElements: The captioned lookbook spread (page.tsx §#radovi, lav.module.css .frame/.crop): five photographs with real shade names underneath ("Maslinasta i čokolada", "Mliječni french", "Paleta LUXIO"), every second frame dropped 2.5rem (`index % 2 === 1 ? "sm:mt-10"`). One line of logic turns a product grid into a magazine spread. This is the page's subject-grounded signature: the business sells colour, so the page is built around a colour catalogue.

The single lacquer red (--lav-red #c81d31, lav.module.css). It is the booking button and nothing else that is chrome — beyond that it appears only as typographic marks: the desktop kicker, the 1/2/3 booking numerals, the underline under the phone number, the 01–06 tile numbers, the Instagram glyph in the phone rail. Colour is used as an instruction, not as decoration.

The trust rule (page.tsx §"Zašto LavLav"): the studio's three own bio claims — LUXIO, 200+ boja, 2 nedjelje garancije — set in the display face inside one section-wide band divided by vertical hairlines. It does the job of a stat block or three badge pills with no pills, no numbers-as-hero, no icons.

The phone-only service menu (page.tsx lines 179–206): six native `<details>` tiles in a 2×3 hairline grid, each a min-h-28 tap target with a `+` that rotates 45° on open and an `open:bg-[--lav-shell]` fill. It reads like a salon menu card, and it exists *because* six full descriptions would otherwise make services the longest section on a phone — the comment in the file says exactly that.

The passe-partout map plate (page.tsx §#kontakt, MapEmbed.tsx): the map sits inside a `border p-1.5` mat like a framed print, and the frame is empty graph paper drawn in `currentColor` until the visitor presses "Prikaži mapu" — no Google request, no asset, and it inherits any palette.

The phone action rail (page.tsx lines 405–436): a two-cell fixed footer where the primary cell is labelled with the actual booking system ("DIKIDI / Rezerviši termin") and the second shows the literal handle @lavlav.mne. The destination is named before the tap. The hero CTAs are `hidden md:flex`, so the rail replaces them rather than duplicating them.
typography: Two faces, one job each. Tenor Sans (`--font-lav-display`, single weight 400, next/font with latin-ext for č/ć/š/ž/đ) is the display voice — the stacked LAV/LAV wordmark at 0.2em tracking, all section headings at `clamp(1.75rem,4vw,2.5rem)`, service titles, the trust claims, the step numerals, the phone number, even the `+` affordance. Plus Jakarta Sans carries body, labels, and every button. There is one label token reused everywhere — `text-[0.68rem] uppercase tracking-[0.26em]` — for kickers, captions, nav, and meta, so all the small type in the page is literally the same object. Hierarchy comes from face contrast + scale + tracking, not from a weight ramp: body is one size, muted grey, ~65ch max-width (`max-w-xs`/`max-w-md`/`max-w-sm` used as measure limits), and almost nothing is bold except buttons and link text. Headings are restrained — the h1 tops out around 3.2rem, so nothing shouts.
color: Five tokens, scoped to the route in lav.module.css: cream #f2eee5 (paper), shell #e8e2d6 (second stock), ink #111, muted #5c5751, line #d8d1c4, plus one red #c81d31. Contrast is documented in the file (muted 6.2:1 on cream; red 4.9:1 on cream and white-on-red 5.7:1) — the palette was checked, not vibed. Deployment: cream is the default ground; shell appears exactly once, as the full-bleed gallery band, so section rhythm comes from a paper change rather than from cards; hairlines in --lav-line do all remaining structural work. Red is rationed to the booking action and small typographic marks. On the phone hero the palette inverts locally — white text over a `linear-gradient(180deg, rgba(17,17,17,.04) 30%, rgba(17,17,17,.88))` scrim — and the kicker flips from red to white/80 there, which is the only palette exception on the page.
composition: Hero (desktop): asymmetric split `lg:grid-cols-[1.05fr_0.95fr]`, text left, a 30rem photograph right, with the caption "VRIJEME ZA TEBE" hung *below the photo's right edge* (`lg:-bottom-8 lg:right-0`) instead of inside it — the one unexpected move in an otherwise conventional split.

Hero (phone/tablet): same markup, different composition — the figure goes `absolute inset-0` behind a scrim and the copy is bottom-anchored over it as a full-bleed cover; at `sm` it gains a bordered frame with an inset margin (`sm:mx-8 sm:border`) so on tablet it reads as a plated image rather than an edge-to-edge banner.
Trust rule: full-width band, `border-y`, three equal cells with `sm:border-l` dividers — the page's only horizontally-divided row, and it lands immediately after the hero as a hard break.

Services (desktop): heading left, a right-aligned explanatory note ("the full price list lives on DIKIDI") on the same baseline via `items-end justify-between`; below it a 3-column `dl` where each entry has only a top hairline. Deliberately quiet — the section refuses to be a card grid.

Services (phone): entirely different object — a 2×3 tap-to-open tile grid built with `border-l border-t` on the container and `border-b border-r` on the cells, so the grid is drawn once with no double lines.

Lookbook: shell-ground band, `-mx-5` full-bleed scroll strip on phone at 78% frame width so the next photo peeks, becoming a 2/3-column staggered grid at sm/lg with alternating 2.5rem offsets and 4:5 crops.
Booking: asymmetric `lg:grid-cols-[0.85fr_1.15fr]` — argument and CTA in the narrow left column, three steps in the wider right column, so the block is weighted rather than centred.

Contact: two columns of unequal texture — typographic left (address, red-underlined phone at `underline-offset-8`, two hairline handle rows with right-aligned meta labels) against a single large framed plate on the right.
Density shifts intentionally: hero and gallery are photo-heavy and airy; services and contact are dense typographic blocks; the trust rule is a thin hard line between them.
interaction: Lookbook hover crop: `transform: scale(1.04)` over 0.5s on a `cubic-bezier(.16,1,.3,1)`, gated behind `@media (hover:hover) and (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)`. This is the ONLY thing on the page that moves unasked, and the CSS comment says so explicitly. Earns its place — it is on the subject (the nails) and it hints the frames are inspectable.

Phone lookbook: `scroll-snap-type: x mandatory` with hidden scrollbars and a matching `scroll-padding-left: 1.25rem` so the first frame snaps to the text rail rather than the viewport edge (a real bug the file documents fixing). Reader-driven — no autoplay, no dots. Earns its place.

Service tiles: native `<details>/<summary>` with a `group-open:rotate-45` plus sign and an open-state background change; `motion-reduce:transition-none`. Zero JavaScript, correct semantics, and the affordance is labelled in words ("Dodirni za detalje"). Earns its place.

Map: click-to-load — the iframe is not built until the visitor presses the button (MapEmbed.tsx), with a plain Google Maps link underneath that costs no request. The page's only client component. Earns its place on privacy and LCP grounds.
No scroll-reveals, no fade-ins, no parallax, no counters anywhere on the page.

Focus is a single shared token — `focus-visible:outline-2 outline-offset-4 outline-[--lav-red]` — applied to every interactive element including the wordmark, with an inset variant on the dark sticky rail. Touch targets are consistently min-h-11/12/14/16.
mobile: At 390px it is not a narrowed desktop — three sections are re-authored. The hero becomes a full-bleed cover photo with the headline sitting on it; the six services become a tap-to-expand 2×3 tile menu instead of a stack of six paragraphs; the gallery becomes a snap strip at 78% frame width so the next photo peeks; and both hero buttons disappear because a fixed two-cell rail (DIKIDI booking + @lavlav.mne) has taken over the CTA job — so there is never a duplicate CTA on screen. The body gets `pb-[calc(5rem+env(safe-area-inset-bottom))]` and the rail `pb-[env(safe-area-inset-bottom)]`, so nothing hides under the rail or the home indicator. What holds it together is that the type system, the hairlines and the single red are unchanged across breakpoints: only composition changes, never the language. One real flaw at this width — the third trust claim ("2 nedjelje garancije") is not visible in the 390px capture between "200+ boja" and the CTA band, so the stacked trust rule appears to be truncated or overlapped and should be checked.

transferableIdeas.idea: Re-author the longest phone section instead of stacking it — ship two different components for the same data, toggled at one breakpoint.
transferableIdeas.why: The failure mode of a small-business page is always one section that becomes an endless phone scroll (six services, twelve dishes, nine treatments). Building a compact tap-to-reveal object for phone and a quiet typographic list for desktop is the single change that makes a page feel designed for the device rather than reflowed onto it. Here it is `<details>` tiles vs a `<dl>` (page.tsx 179–230).
transferableIdeas.howToTransfer: Find the section with the most repeated items. On phone render titles only in a 2-column tap grid; on pointer render the full item + description list. Use native `<details>` so it costs no JS and stays accessible. Rule of thumb: apply it when items × description lines > ~10 lines on a phone.

transferableIdeas.idea: Rescue the hero photo as a phone cover: same `<figure>`, `absolute inset-0` + gradient scrim + bottom-anchored copy on phone, `lg:static` split on desktop.
transferableIdeas.why: A split hero shrunk to 390px becomes a small photo above a text block — the most generic result possible. Repositioning the same element makes the phone view feel authored, and it costs no extra markup or image.
transferableIdeas.howToTransfer: Wrap the copy in an `absolute inset-x-0 bottom-0 z-10 … lg:static` block, the photo in a figure with `absolute inset-0 … lg:relative`, and put a top-transparent→88%-ink gradient in between. Flip the accent-coloured kicker to white at that breakpoint. Only use it when the photograph has a calm bottom third — otherwise crop or dim harder.

transferableIdeas.idea: Name the destination in the sticky action bar, and delete the hero CTAs at the same breakpoint.
transferableIdeas.why: "Kontaktiraj nas" tells the visitor nothing; "DIKIDI / Rezerviši termin" and the literal @handle tell them exactly what will open. And because the rail and the hero buttons hand off at the identical breakpoint, the page never shows two competing primary CTAs at once — the usual sticky-bar mistake.
transferableIdeas.howToTransfer: Two cells, asymmetric grid (`grid-cols-[1.45fr_1fr]`), primary in the accent, secondary on paper with a hairline divider. Each cell = a small uppercase system name over a bold action line. Pair with `md:hidden` on the rail and `hidden md:flex` on the hero buttons, plus safe-area padding on both.

transferableIdeas.idea: One saturated colour with exactly one functional job, plus a 4-value neutral ramp.
transferableIdeas.why: Restricting the accent to the booking action means the eye finds the conversion without any element having to be large or loud, and it makes the page look art-directed rather than themed. The small typographic marks (numerals, an underline, a kicker) read as the same ink, not as decoration.
transferableIdeas.howToTransfer: Pick the accent from the product itself (here: nail lacquer; elsewhere: a sauce, a stone, a jersey, a safety colour). Declare 5–6 tokens in a route-scoped CSS module and write the measured contrast ratio next to each in a comment. Then audit: if the accent appears on anything that is not the primary action or a typographic mark, remove it.

transferableIdeas.idea: One-line editorial stagger on a photo grid: `index % 2 === 1 → sm:mt-10`.
transferableIdeas.why: It breaks the identical-row rhythm that makes gallery grids read as e-commerce, for zero structural complexity, and it survives responsive changes because it is a margin, not a position.
transferableIdeas.howToTransfer: Any grid of 4–8 photographs of comparable importance. Fix a single aspect ratio (4:5 here) so the stagger, not the crop, creates the variation. Turn it off at the phone breakpoint where the grid becomes a strip.

transferableIdeas.idea: Replace the stat block with a full-bleed claims rule: 2–4 of the business's own phrases, set in the display face, in one bordered band with vertical dividers.
transferableIdeas.why: It delivers the reassurance a stat strip is supposed to deliver — brand, scale, guarantee — with no pills, no icons, no invented numbers, and it doubles as a hard structural break between the hero and the body of the page.
transferableIdeas.howToTransfer: Take the phrases verbatim from the business's own bio/menu/window (`trustLine` in data.ts is literally their Instagram bio). `border-y` on the section, `sm:grid-cols-3`, `sm:border-l` on all but the first, display face at ~1.125rem with slight positive tracking. Never write the claims yourself.

transferableIdeas.idea: A hard motion budget: exactly one unrequested animation per page, on the subject, gated by `(hover:hover) and (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)`.
transferableIdeas.why: Scattered scroll-reveals are the loudest tell of a generated page. Spending the entire motion budget on a 4% crop of the product photography makes the restraint itself feel like a decision — and everything else on the page is reader-driven (snap strip, details, map button).
transferableIdeas.howToTransfer: Before adding any animation, ask what the page's one moving thing is. Put it on the subject photography or the primary control, cap it at ~4% / ~500ms with an ease-out curve, and gate it in CSS not JS. Everything else moves only in response to a tap.

transferableIdeas.idea: Caption every photograph with a real, specific noun in the small-caps label token.
transferableIdeas.why: "Maslinasta i čokolada" / "Paleta LUXIO" turn a gallery into a catalogue with a voice; the visitor learns vocabulary they can use when booking. Uncaptioned photo grids look like stock, and captions cost nothing.
transferableIdeas.howToTransfer: Store the caption next to the src in the data file (see `lookbook` in data.ts, which also keeps a `source` field for provenance that is never rendered). Use the same uppercase/tracked label token as the kickers so captions are typographically part of the system.

transferableIdeas.idea: Let the business's existing system own its own data — link, don't duplicate.
transferableIdeas.why: The page deliberately shows service *categories* and points the price list at DIKIDI, with the reason written in the code ("duplicating it here would be wrong within a month"). This is simultaneously the honest choice, the cheaper build, and the cleaner design — it is why the services section can be six short lines instead of a price table.
transferableIdeas.howToTransfer: Identify what the client already maintains elsewhere (booking system, delivery menu, Instagram, a PDF price list) and design the section as an editorial summary plus a labelled hand-off, not a copy. It removes the biggest maintenance risk in a small-business site and usually removes the ugliest block too.

transferableIdeas.idea: Click-to-load third-party embed behind a placeholder drawn in `currentColor`.
transferableIdeas.why: Kills a privacy leak and a large render-blocking third-party payload, and the graph-paper placeholder needs no asset and inherits any palette — so one component works across every demo in the repo (MapEmbed.tsx).
transferableIdeas.howToTransfer: `repeating-linear-gradient` grid at ~15% opacity, a one-line note explaining what will load, a real `<button>` that mounts the iframe, and a plain link to the same destination that costs no request. Same pattern for YouTube, Instagram embeds, chat widgets and map providers.

weaknesses: The desktop services `dl` (page.tsx 221–230) is a hairline-topped 3-column list — the closest thing on the page to the banned 'AI editorial' grammar. It survives only because there are six entries, they are one line each, and the display face carries them. Do not transfer it as a default section pattern; it would collapse into slop with ten items or longer copy.

The 01–06 numbering on the phone service tiles is decorative sequence numbering, exactly the idiom the house standard rejects. It is tolerable here because it doubles as a grid index for a tap menu, but it should not be copied to any section that is not a numbered grid of controls.

The 1 / 2 / 3 booking section is a conventional three-step explainer and is the least distinctive block on the page; the big red numerals are the only thing keeping it from being a generic 'how it works' row. Reuse the asymmetric 0.85/1.15 column split, not the three-step device.

On desktop the contact section's right column is a large, mostly empty graph-paper rectangle. The click-to-load principle is right; the visual result is the weakest composition on the page. A smaller plate, or a photograph of the entrance with the map below it, would carry that column better.

The phone hero legibility depends entirely on a heavy 88%-ink scrim over the photograph. It works with this warm, dark-bottomed image; drop in a bright or busy photo and the white headline fails. Do not transfer the scrim without checking the specific image, and never as a fixed value.

The 390px capture appears to lose the third trust claim ('2 nedjelje garancije') between the stacked band and the CTA — the stacked trust rule looks truncated or overlapped at that width. Verify before treating the trust-rule pattern as finished.

Both service renderings ship in the DOM (one `md:hidden`, one `hidden md:grid`), so all six descriptions exist twice in the HTML. Acceptable at this size, but the duplication is a maintenance and payload cost that grows with content — do not scale the two-component technique to a long list without moving the data into a shared render.

The desktop hero is otherwise a fairly standard left-text/right-photo split with a lot of empty cream to its left; only the caption hung under the photo's right edge lifts it. It is the section with the least invention on the page.
